ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Sicily Channel is located on the African plate northern continental margin, also referred to as the Pelagian domain, which is part of the foreland of the Maghrebides south-verging chain (Corti et al., 2006). This zone is considered as an example of continental rift (e.g. Civile et al., 2010). Seismic reflection profiles show the presence of diffuse normal faulting associated with the formation of grabens and half grabens. The main grabens are filled with sediments as thick as more than 1000 m like, for example the Linosa and Pantelleria grabens (Torelli et al., 1995; Finetti and Del Ben, 2005; Civile et al., 2010). The crust, in correspondence with the rift structure, is relatively thinned to thicknesses of 17-25 km (Finetti and Del Ben, 2005). The tectonic activity is accompanied by volcanism and magmatism, and recent fault activity is demonstrated by displaced Late Pliocene â€“ Quaternary deposits (Civile et al., 2010).
Geodetic data indicate independent motion of the Pelagian domain with respect to Nubia with NE-SW oriented 1.5 mm/y extension and a 1.7 mm/y dextral strike-slip component (Serpelloni et al., 2007). Instrumental seismicity is rather sparse and of moderate, M<5 magnitude, while historical records are missing due to the far offshore position of the area. Available focal mechanisms (European-Mediterranean RCMT catalog; Pondrelli et al., 2006; 2007; 2011) indicate NW-SE oriented compression, resulting in a predominant right-lateral strike-slip motion on generally E-W oriented fault planes. Such structural and kinematic framework is also supported by geologic studies (Reuther and Eisbacher, 1985; Reuther, 1990) which show that the NW-SE trending grabens are connected by E-W trending dextral strike-slip faults.
This Source represents the N bounding Malta graben active fault. The depth range of the Source was estimated from seismic profile data (Civile et al., 2010), including data on the thinned crust depth in the Sicily Channel with respect to the surrounding lithosphere (Finetti and Del Ben, 2005). Strike and dip were estimated from the geophysical data (Torelli et al., 1995; Corti et al., 2006), while rake was estimated from geological considerations of slip direction on fault plane in the current stress regime (Serpelloni et al., 2007; Heidbach et al., 2010) coupled with existing regional seismological data (Pondrelli et al., 2006; 2011). Slip rate values were obtained by partitioning the geodetic rates (Serpelloni et al., 2007) among the adjacent Sources, considering that one of them has significantly greater vertical throw (Corti et al., 2006). The maximum magnitude was estimated based on the source geometry, regional geological and geodynamic considerations.
